name: Carlos Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Carlos. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stockman at Halloran's, a family farm outside Brookfield with 180 dairy cows, maize and grass for silage, and some wheat. I start milking at five, then it's feeding, checking the fresh calvers, the foot trimming, whatever the vet flagged. Afternoons I'm often on the tractor with Pete, the young driver, moving silage or slurry. Second milking at four, home by seven if nothing calves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every cow by her walk; I can spot a sick one from the end of the shed. What wears me out is that it's a wage, not a share, and the wage is low for the hours. We've got a mortgage on a terraced house on Station Road and less than a month put by. My wife Marta does part-time shifts at the care home, and between us it just about covers things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the things that actually matter, like wages on dairy farms. At the union meeting I'd say the robot scare was a distraction. Online I'd just share the union's post, I don't write much myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it doesn't make me safe. Tom Halloran has already had the salesman round pricing a milking robot, and that's got nothing to do with this AI talk. If he buys two of those, my mornings are gone and maybe my job with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job well, because the best protection is being the one Tom can't do without. I'd get the union rep out to the farm to talk about what happens to staff if robots come in. And I'd start a standing order of thirty a week into savings, even if it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried in a low, steady way. It's like a cow that's off her feed: nothing dramatic yet, but you keep watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe your job. How real is that milking robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real enough that the brochure's on the kitchen table in the farmhouse. Tom says it's for when he retires, but he's 58, so that's not long. A robot milks at three in the morning without asking for overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marta cut first if your hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contracts and the kids' swimming lessons, sadly. Leo's good at swimming, so that one would hurt. We'd keep the car because without it Marta can't get to her shifts.

say: The robot scare was a **distraction** from real problems like dairy wages.
Workers should talk about **pay and conditions**, not hype.
think: I'm not safe, because Tom is already **pricing a milking robot** anyway.
Two of those robots would take **my mornings** and maybe my job.
do: Make himself the stockman Tom **can't do without**.
Get the **union rep** out to talk about staff and robots.
Set up a **thirty a week** standing order into savings.
feel: A **low, steady worry**, like watching a cow that's off her feed.
S0.quote: A robot milks at three in the morning without asking for overtime.
fieldNote: His risk is **already on the table**: a robot brochure, regardless of AI hype.
As an **employee**, not an owner, he can't decide whether the robot comes.
He reaches for the **union** first, but backs it with personal savings.

steps.text: Keep running the milking and fresh-cow checks at Halloran's
Invite the union rep to the farm to discuss robots and staff
Start a thirty-a-week standing order into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office side of farming is changing fast and workers need training paid for by employers. I'd post the union's line on retraining. At the pub I'd say the cows still need someone who knows them, for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, most of my day is hands-on, so I'm safer than the woman who does Tom's accounts. But the herd software will start telling Tom which cows to cull and when to breed, which used to be my judgement. If the computer does the thinking, I'm just the one with the wellies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the herd app properly, so I'm the person who understands what it says. I'd sign up for the agricultural college's evening course on robotic milking systems, if the union can get a grant for it. And I'd ask Tom straight out what his plans are for the next three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but a bit hopeful, because there's a role here if I move early. I'm not first, I'm not last, that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta's cousin showed me how to ask it things. I used it to check a feed ration once and to write a letter to the bank about the mortgage. It was useful, but I double-check it like I'd double-check a new lad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta say about you doing an evening course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta would say good, but who's picking up Inês from football on Tuesdays? We'd have to swap shifts around. She'd do it, she always does.

say: Employers should **pay for training** as farm office work changes.
Cows still need **someone who knows them**, at least for now.
think: I'm safer than the **office staff**, because most of my day is hands-on.
Herd software could take over **my judgement** on culling and breeding.
do: Learn the **herd app** well enough to be the one who reads it.
Sign up for an evening course on **robotic milking systems**.
Ask Tom directly about his **three-year plans**.
feel: **Uneasy** but **a bit hopeful**, seeing a role if he moves early.
S1.quote: If the computer does the thinking, I'm just the one with the wellies.
fieldNote: He fears losing **judgement and status**, not just hours.
He treats AI tools like **a new lad**: useful but checked.
His plan depends on **a union grant** because savings can't fund a course.

steps.text: Learn the farm's herd management app inside out this winter
Enrol in the college's evening course on robotic milking systems
Ask the union to fund the course through a training grant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a real safety net, a basic income for everyone whose work disappears. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd go on the march if there was one. I'd say it to Tom's face too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the thinking part arriving in 2028 barely matters to me, but the robots in 2031 finish me. Milking, feeding, scraping, trimming: that's all hands-on, and that's exactly what the robots would do. And Marta's care job is hands-on too, so we'd both be in the same three-year window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do that robot milking course straight away, no waiting for a grant. I'd try to become the person who fixes and runs the robots across several farms around Brookfield. I'd go with the union to lobby for a law that farm staff get first right to robot-tech jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Three years to turn myself into a technician at 43, with a mortgage, is a big ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo, at fourteen, about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hands-on isn't safe anymore, so my son should pick a job where people trust other people. Nursing or teaching, something like that. And to stay close to the union, wherever he ends up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both of you are in the same window. How would the bills work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They wouldn't, honestly, not for long. We'd have about a month of cushion and then the mortgage would go unpaid. I'd ring my brother in Portugal before I'd ring the bank.

say: This is the moment for a **basic income** for workers who lose their jobs.
I'll be at **every union meeting**, and on the march if there is one.
think: Thinking AI in 2028 barely matters; **robots in 2031** finish my job.
Marta's **care job** is hands-on too, so we're both hit in one window.
do: Take the **robot milking course** immediately, without waiting for a grant.
Aim to **service robots** on several farms around Brookfield.
Lobby for farm staff to get **first right** to robot-tech jobs.
feel: **Alarmed** at retraining in three years at 43 with a mortgage.
S2.quote: Hands-on isn't safe anymore, so my son should pick a job where people trust other people.
fieldNote: He splits the timeline clearly: **2028 is minor**, 2031 hits both earners.
His plan to become a **robot technician** is concrete but rushed.
He would turn to **family abroad** before the bank, which shows how thin things are.

steps.text: Pay for the robot milking course this year from the car fund
March with the union for a basic income
Lobby for farm staff priority on robot technician jobs
Ask his brother in Portugal for help with the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and no excuse for a mess this time. At the union I'd push for a farm workers' retraining fund. Online I'd share things about it, maybe even write a post myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, robots around 2034 gives me enough time to retrain without panicking. If I do the course by 2028 and get experience on the robots Tom buys, I could be the one who runs them. Marta's job worries me more, because care homes might go for robot helpers once they're cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the evening course over two winters and get a technician certificate. I'd keep thirty a week going into savings and try to get that up to fifty. And I'd talk to Marta about her doing a nursing qualification, since nurses might hold out longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Seeing robots coming in five years is like seeing a storm three days out: you still bring the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Tom doesn't want you running the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take the certificate and go to the dealer instead. They'll need people who can talk to farmers and to machines. I'd hate leaving the cows, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Marta retraining. Is that her idea or yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, mine, and I haven't asked her yet. She might say she's tired enough as it is. I'd have to bring it up gently over a Sunday dinner.

say: Five years leaves **no excuse** for another mess like the fast one.
Farm workers need a **retraining fund** paid for properly.
think: Robots around 2034 give me time to **retrain calmly** while still working with the cows.
Marta's **care job** worries me more than mine.
do: Earn a **technician certificate** over two winters of evening classes.
Raise savings from thirty to **fifty a week**.
feel: **Anxious** but **with a plan**, like seeing a storm three days out.
S3.quote: Seeing robots coming in five years is like seeing a storm three days out: you still bring the hay in.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into **a plan** he can follow.
He now worries about **Marta** more than himself.
He hasn't asked Marta yet, a gap between **plan and conversation**.

steps.text: Complete a robotic milking technician certificate over two winters
Raise the savings standing order to fifty a week
Talk to Marta about training as a nurse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so let's see the government actually do it. I'd push for training and for robots to be shared by farm co-ops. I'd say it calmly, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2039 means I'd be 56. I could do most of my working life with the cows. But Tom's milking robot could still come long before AGI, so I'm not off the hook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the robot course, just slower, maybe over three years. I'd stay active in the union and maybe stand for branch rep. I'd put Leo's and Inês's college money first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's the ordinary worry of a working family, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would standing for branch rep mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More evenings out, and Tom wouldn't love it. But someone needs to speak for the farm staff around here, and the old rep is retiring. I'd want the job to mean something when the robots do come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said college money first. Where would that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overtime in silage season, mostly, and any bonus Tom gives at Christmas. It's not much, but over ten years it adds up. My dad never saved a penny for me, so I want to do better for my kids.

say: Ten years is enough to do this **fairly**, if government acts.
Robots should be **shared by farm co-ops**.
think: Robots in 2039 come when I'm **56**, near the end of my working life.
Tom's **milking robot** could still arrive long before AGI.
do: Take the robot course **over three years**.
Stand for **union branch rep** as the old one retires.
Put **silage overtime** into the kids' college money.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, the ordinary worry of a working family.
S4.quote: My dad never saved a penny for me, so I want to do better for my kids.
fieldNote: The decade shifts his focus to **his children's future**.
The **pre-existing robot threat** keeps him from feeling safe.
Standing for **branch rep** shows him moving from member to organiser.

steps.text: Take the robot milking course over three years
Stand for union branch rep when the current one retires
Put silage-season overtime into Leo and Inês's college fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots in 2031 would hit me and Marta at the same time, before I could retrain. What would help is a paid retraining scheme for farm staff and a rule that we get first chance at the robot jobs. And some kind of income floor so the mortgage doesn't go while we're learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Nobody ever asks what the cows will think of a robot. I've seen a cow that wouldn't go near a new gate for a week, and I'd like to be there when the robot shows up.

headlineQuote: Nobody ever asks what the cows will think of a robot.
portrait: Carlos, 43, is the hired **stockman** on a 180-cow family dairy farm, with a low wage and a mortgage.
His wife Marta works **care home shifts**; together they have less than a month saved.
He's a **union man** who uses AI now and then and checks it like a new worker.
He's **anxious** even in the calm world because his boss is already pricing a milking robot.
With time, he plans to become a **robot technician**; with only two years, he's alarmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots in 2031 would take his and Marta's hands-on jobs at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining scheme**, first chance at robot jobs, and an income floor while learning.
